title: Word Ladder II
statement:
A *ladder* from `beginWord` to `endWord` is a list of words that starts with `beginWord` and ends with `endWord`, in which every word after the first is taken from `wordList`, and any two consecutive words differ at exactly one letter position. `beginWord` itself does not have to be in `wordList`.

Return all ladders that have the fewest words, each written out in full as `[beginWord, ..., endWord]`. The ladders may be returned in any order. If no ladder exists, return an empty list.
constraints: beginWord, endWord and every wordList[i] use only lowercase English letters
The words in wordList are distinct
All shortest ladders together hold at most 10^5 words
signature: List<List<String>> findLadders(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList)
notes:
## Intuition

Every word is a node, and two words are linked when they differ in one position. The shortest ladders are the shortest paths from `beginWord` to `endWord` in this graph. Enumerating every path and keeping the shortest is exponential. Breadth-first search reaches words in order of distance, so if each word remembers which words of the previous layer led to it, the shortest ladders can be rebuilt afterwards by walking those links back from `endWord`.

## Approach

1. Put `wordList` in a set `unvisited`. If `endWord` is missing, return `[]`. Remove `beginWord` so it is never revisited.
2. Group the dictionary into `buckets` keyed by a `pattern` with one position blanked out (`lo*` holds `lot` and `log`). Words sharing a pattern are exactly one letter apart.
3. Process one BFS layer `level` at a time. For each `word` and each position, every word in the matching bucket is a `candidate` neighbour.
4. If the candidate is still unvisited, record `word` as one of its parents in `next`. A word may collect several parents from the same layer.
5. Only after the whole layer is done, remove the new words from `unvisited` and store their parents in `parents`. Stop once `endWord` was reached (`found`).
6. `backtrack` from `endWord` through `parents`, pushing words on `path`; at `beginWord`, reverse a copy of `path` into `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

The buckets include `*ot` = `[hot, dot, lot]` and `*og` = `[dog, log, cog]`. Layers from `hit`: `[hot]` (through `h*t`), then `[dot, lot]` (both with parent `hot`), then `[dog, log]`, then `[cog]` with parents `dog` and `log`. Backtracking from `cog` gives `cog, dog, dot, hot, hit` and `cog, log, lot, hot, hit`; reversed, these are the two answers.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N · L²) to build the patterns and run the search, where N is the number of words and L their length (each pattern costs O(L) to build), plus the total size of the output for backtracking.
- Space: O(N · L²) for the buckets, plus the parent lists and the output.

## Pitfalls

- Removing a word from `unvisited` the moment it is first reached loses its other parents in the same layer, and with them some ladders.
- Keep searching layers only until `endWord` appears; deeper ladders are longer.
- `beginWord` may also appear in `wordList`; delete it first so no ladder returns to it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `unvisited` | dictionary words not yet placed in any layer |
| `buckets` | pattern with one blank position → words that fit it |
| `pattern` | a word with position `i` replaced by `*` |
| `level` | the current BFS layer |
| `next` | words of the next layer, each with its list of parents |
| `parents` | for every reached word, the words one step closer to `beginWord` |
| `found` | whether `endWord` has been reached |
| `path` | the ladder being rebuilt, from `endWord` backwards |
| `result` | all shortest ladders |
